strengths: Compelling and practical motivation: training search-based agents like AlphaZero requires immense computational resources due to MCTS rollouts during data generation, and demonstrating that a pure model-free approach can achieve superior sample efficiency in the moderate-resource regime is of significant interest to the RL and games community.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across five diverse board games (Animal Shogi, Gardner Chess, 9x9 Go, Hex, and Othello) as well as an exploration on 19x19 Go, showing consistent efficiency gains in simulator evaluations over AlphaZero variants, DQN, and PPO.

Thorough and insightful ablation studies (Figure 6) systematically isolating each component (reverse KL regularization, entropy regularization, and intermediate lambda-returns), confirming that all three are critical to prevent policy collapse or high variance.

Extensive supplementary analyses addressing key practical concerns, including hyperparameter sensitivity (Appendix D), test-time search scaling with MCTS (Appendix H), rollout budget tuning for AlphaZero baselines (Appendix G), and wall-clock verification (Table 7).
Clear, well-structured presentation and commendable intellectual honesty regarding limitations, particularly acknowledging asymptotic performance trade-offs versus massive-scale search methods.
weaknesses: Algorithmic and theoretical novelty is relatively modest: the closed-form regularized policy update combining entropy and reverse KL divergence is well-established in regularized MDP and Quantal Response Equilibrium literature (e.g., Sokota et al., 2022; Vieillard et al., 2020), and using lambda-returns with an action-value function is standard RL.

In the main comparative evaluations (Figure 5), search-based methods (AlphaZero, Gumbel AlphaZero) are evaluated purely reactively without test-time search. Because AlphaZero's primary strength is explicitly coupled with search-based planning at inference, evaluating them solely in the reactive regime can underestimate their trained capability, even though Appendix H partially mitigates this by evaluating test-time search on 9x9 Go.

Evaluation in the main paper relies predominantly on win rates against a single fixed anchor opponent from Pgx rather than full round-robin tournaments or multi-engine Elo rankings across all five games, which limits understanding of transitive playing strength and exploitability against varied play styles.

Scalability evidence on full 19x19 Go remains preliminary: the experiments terminate at 800M evaluations where both KLENT and AlphaZero achieve ~50% win rates against the baseline, leaving open whether model-free Q-value learning can scale effectively to grandmaster-level play on large combinatorial board spaces.

strengths: Clear and compelling motivation: Look-ahead search (MCTS) in AlphaZero-style algorithms constitutes the primary computational bottleneck during self-play data generation. Investigating whether model-free reinforcement learning can match or exceed search-based methods under limited computational budgets is an important and practically relevant research question.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The proposed method (KLENT) is evaluated across five distinct medium-scale board games (Animal Shogi, Gardner Chess, 9x9 Go, Hex, Othello) as well as 19x19 Go. KLENT shows substantially faster learning in terms of simulator queries compared to standard model-free baselines (PPO, DQN) and search-based methods (AlphaZero, Gumbel AlphaZero).

Thorough ablation studies and analysis: The paper includes rigorous ablations isolating the contribution of each key component (reverse KL regularization, entropy regularization, and intermediate lambda-returns), accompanied by bias-variance trade-off analysis and convergence behavior on simplified games.

Well-structured presentation and reproducibility efforts: The paper provides clear mathematical derivations, architectural details, hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, and comparisons against established engines (GnuGo, Pachi).
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: The regularized policy update combining reverse KL and entropy regularization with closed-form softmax targets is well-established in the literature on regularized MDPs and policy mirror descent (e.g., Vieillard et al., 2020; Sokota et al., 2022). The novelty lies predominantly in its empirical packaging and application to board games rather than fundamental theoretical innovation.

Evaluation metric nuances (Simulator Evaluations vs. Game Transitions): Measuring training efficiency solely in terms of simulator evaluations (NN queries during self-play) strongly favors model-free methods. For a fixed budget of simulator evaluations, an agent using 32-rollout MCTS experiences 1/32nd the number of game steps and parameter updates compared to a model-free agent. While this is a standard computational proxy, reporting training efficiency in terms of total game steps/episodes and full wall-clock training time curves in the main text would provide a more complete picture of the trade-offs.

Asymptotic capability and scaling: While KLENT shows clear advantages in low-to-moderate compute regimes, search-based methods are known to achieve superior asymptotic play given massive scale (as acknowledged in Section 6 and Appendix G.3). Additional discussion on how the action-value function approximation error accumulates in very deep game trees compared to explicit tree search would strengthen the paper.

strengths: Clear motivation addressing a well-known limitation of search-based RL (e.g., AlphaZero), which suffers from high computational overhead due to Monte Carlo tree search rollouts during training self-play.
Comprehensive empirical testing across five diverse board games (Animal Shogi, Gardner Chess, 9x9 Go, Hex, Othello) as well as preliminary scaling experiments on 19x19 Go.
Thorough ablation study systematically evaluating each component of the algorithm (KL regularization, entropy regularization, and intermediate λ-returns).
Extensive supplementary material providing hyperparameter sensitivity analyses, test-time search scaling (Appendix H), and wall-clock inference measurements.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: The proposed update rule (Equation 3) is a direct closed-form solution to the standard reverse KL and entropy regularized policy objective, which is well-studied in regularized MDP literature (e.g., Vieillard et al., 2020; Sokota et al., 2022; Zhan et al., 2023). Combining this analytical update with standard λ-returns provides an incremental methodological advance.

Potential evaluation bias from using single anchored opponents: In two-player zero-sum games, measuring progress solely via win rate against a single fixed anchor agent can be deceptive due to non-transitivity and cyclic dynamics (Balduzzi et al., 2018). An agent may specialize in exploiting specific flaws of the anchor rather than learning a robust game-theoretic strategy. Broader round-robin tournaments or population-based evaluations in the main text would provide stronger validation.

Metric alignment ('Simulator Evaluations'): Measuring learning efficiency strictly by simulator evaluations (network queries during self-play) inherently disadvantages MCTS methods by a factor equal to the rollout budget (e.g., 32x), while obscuring the number of game episodes, transitions, and environment steps required. In board games where an exact, fast transition model is freely available, discarding lookahead search requires strong justification regarding asymptotic performance, which remains unproven here as conceded in the limitations.

Lack of competitive benchmarking against standard game engines on full-scale games: For 19x19 Go, the agent is trained for a modest budget and evaluated against a single checkpoint, without calibration against established open-source engines (e.g., KataGo, Leela Zero) or full Elo ladders.

strengths: Sound and elegant theoretical contribution: Theorem 5.1 provides a strictly broader convergence region for regularized policy updates in normal-form two-player zero-sum games (\(\alpha(\alpha + 2\beta) > \|R\|_2^2 / 4\)) compared to prior art (e.g., Sokota et al., 2022), with theoretical boundaries closely matching empirical simulations on Matching Pennies.

Strong empirical motivation and performance: The paper demonstrates that a pure model-free regularized RL approach (KLENT) can be stable and achieve substantially higher sample/simulator efficiency (up to 4x) than MCTS-based methods like AlphaZero and Gumbel AlphaZero across five standard board games.

Comprehensive experimental validation and ablations: The evaluation is thorough, including scaling to 19x19 Go, head-to-head matches against traditional Go engines (GnuGo, Pachi), compatibility with test-time MCTS scaling, sensitivity sweeps over hyperparameters, and clear ablations isolating the importance of reverse KL regularization, entropy regularization, and \(\lambda\)-returns.
weaknesses: The fundamental update formulation is not entirely novel, as combinations of reverse-KL and entropy regularization have been explored in policy mirror descent and related literature (e.g., Sokota et al., 2022; Vieillard et al., 2020a); however, the authors appropriately position their work as revisiting and providing new theoretical and empirical characterizations of this update in two-player zero-sum games.

The theoretical convergence guarantee for finite-length games (Theorem C.12) relies on an idealized sequential convergence assumption (backward induction where lower-depth states converge before preceding states), which does not fully capture non-asymptotic dynamics or finite-sample errors encountered under simultaneous neural network updates.

The primary efficiency metric in the main text is simulator evaluations, which inherently penalizes tree search methods that perform internal rollouts per environment step; while the authors partially address wall-clock inference in Appendix M, presenting full end-to-end wall-clock training curves alongside simulator counts would give a more complete picture of practical training speedups.

strengths: Improved theoretical convergence bound: Theorem 5.1 sharpens the local linear convergence condition for regularized self-play in two-player zero-sum normal-form games to $\alpha(\alpha + 2\beta) > \|R\|_2^2 / 4$, strictly expanding the convergence region previously established by Sokota et al. (2022). The phase-diagram experiments on Matching Pennies closely corroborate this theoretical boundary.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The proposed model-free approach (KLENT) is tested across five diverse board games (Animal Shogi, Gardner Chess, 9x9 Go, Hex, and Othello) as well as 19x19 Go, outperforming standard model-free baselines (PPO, DQN, Munchausen DQN, GRPO) and demonstrating high sample efficiency relative to search-based methods under equal simulator budgets.

Rigorous ablations and sensitivity analysis: The paper includes systematic ablations isolating the specific roles of reverse-KL regularization, entropy regularization, and intermediate $\lambda$-returns, supported by a 27-point grid sensitivity analysis and network architecture comparisons in the appendix.

Transparent presentation: The manuscript is clearly written, organized, and explicit regarding its scope, acknowledging that the primary goal is not introducing completely new primitives but characterizing and combining reverse-KL, entropy regularization, and $\lambda$-returns for sample-efficient game playing.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic originality: The core policy update rule (Equation 3) is a direct analytical consequence of reverse-KL and Shannon entropy regularization, which has appeared in closely related forms in policy mirror descent, Munchausen RL (Vieillard et al., 2020a,b), and quantal response equilibrium dynamics (Sokota et al., 2022). The algorithmic novelty is therefore modest.

Idealized assumptions in the finite-horizon game analysis: Theorem C.12 relies on backward induction where the action-value function is assumed to have fully converged at state depth $k$ before updating depth $k+1$. In the practical deep RL algorithm (KLENT), policy and value networks are trained simultaneously across all game phases via gradient descent with function approximation, leaving a notable gap between the idealized theorem and the practical setting.

Primary reliance on simulator evaluations as efficiency metric: The main efficiency claim (up to 4x higher efficiency) is based on the number of simulator evaluations. While standard in certain literature, this metric naturally penalizes search-based baselines (MCTS) that query the simulator during forward search per decision, whereas model-free methods consume more policy/value network optimization updates per environment transition.

Evaluation against a single anchored opponent: The primary training curves in Figures 5, 6, and 10 evaluate win rates against a single fixed baseline checkpoint from Pgx / ElfOpenGo. In multi-agent zero-sum settings with non-transitive dynamics, high win rates against a single fixed opponent do not always correspond to monotonic reduction in exploitability or global policy strength, though test-time MCTS evaluations and head-to-head matches against Pachi/GnuGo in the appendix partially alleviate this concern.

strengths: The paper is exceptionally well-written, structured logically, and addresses an important problem in two-player zero-sum games: bridging the gap between computationally expensive search-based methods (AlphaZero) and lightweight model-free RL.

The theoretical analysis is clean and rigorous. Theorem 5.1 / C.8 improves the convergence condition over prior work (Sokota et al., 2022) for two-player zero-sum normal-form games by showing that $\alpha(\alpha + 2\beta) > \|R\|_2^2 / 4$ suffices, and Theorem C.12 provides an intuitive and solid backward-induction proof for finite-length games.

The empirical evaluation is thorough across five standard board game environments (Animal Shogi, Gardner Chess, 9x9 Go, Hex, Othello) as well as full-scale 19x19 Go, demonstrating up to 4x gains in sample efficiency over Gumbel AlphaZero.

The ablations (Figures 7-9) convincingly validate each algorithmic component: reverse-KL regularization for gradual policy updates, entropy regularization to prevent policy collapse/premature convergence, and $\lambda$-returns for balancing bias and variance in value estimation.

The appendix provides extensive and thoughtful supplementary analysis, including sensitivity analyses, network architecture variations, head-to-head comparisons against external benchmarks (Pachi, GnuGo), and wall-clock inference time benchmarks.
weaknesses: The finite-length game convergence theorem (Theorem C.12) assumes an exact tabular backward-induction setting with converged Q-values at each stage, whereas practical KLENT uses simultaneous updates with function approximation and on-policy data collection. Discussing or formally bounding the propagation of function approximation errors would strengthen the theoretical-to-practical connection.

The primary evaluation relies heavily on win rates against anchored baseline checkpoints from Pgx. While Appendix N provides head-to-head matches in Go and Othello, a complete cross-play round-robin tournament across all methods and games would offer an even more robust assessment against transitive and non-transitive exploitability.

As the authors honestly acknowledge, pure model-free policy optimization may eventually encounter an asymptotic performance ceiling compared to large-budget search-based methods when compute is unconstrained.
